narration: Welcome, esteemed members of the technical panel, jury, and clinical leadership from Happiest Health. We are Team SynapseX from D.B.S Kanpur, and today we are proud to present Chhaya—a Type 2 diabetes digital twin engineered not around speculative marketing claims, but around mathematical rigor, biological fidelity, and radical scientific honesty. In Sanskrit, 'Chhaya' means shadow. That is exactly what our prototype creates: it takes a single, isolated glucose sensor wear, fuses it with the patient's longitudinal electronic health record, and projects a continuous, personalized physiological shadow into the weeks that follow. Over the next twenty-five minutes, we will walk you through our complete Phase 1 submission—from the two-stream multimodal architecture and our differential equation model in JAX, to our pre-registered prediction benchmarks and our three-screen clinical dashboard.

title: The Clinical Paradox of Continuous Glucose Monitoring
section: SECTION A: OPENING & PROBLEM STATEMENT (Slides 1–8)
visual:
- Left Column: The 14-Day Sensor Reality
  - Sensor lifespan: 14 days
  - Cost per unit in India: ~₹4,200 ($50 USD)
  - Annual continuous wear cost: >₹100,000 (~$1,200 USD)
  - Accessibility: <2% of Indian Type 2 diabetics wear CGMs continuously
- Right Column: The 90-Day Clinical Void
  - The patient wears one sensor, receives a PDF report
  - Doctor adjusts therapy based on this single window
  - Months pass without continuous interstitial data
- Central Callout: **"Nobody tells the doctor how old that sensor report has become."**
narration: Let us begin with the stark economic and clinical reality on the ground in India and across the developing world. Continuous glucose monitors like the FreeStyle Libre or Dexcom are transformative diagnostic tools, but they last only fourteen days and cost approximately forty-two hundred rupees per patch. For the overwhelming majority of people living with Type 2 diabetes, continuous, year-round sensor monitoring is financially impossible. What happens in clinical practice? A patient wears a sensor once. They generate an ambulatory glucose profile report. Their physician reviews that report, alters their oral hypoglycemic therapy or insulin regimen, and treats them on the basis of that fourteen-day snapshot for the next three to six months. But biology does not stand still. Lifestyle changes, pancreatic beta-cell fatigue, stress, and medication adjustments continuously shift the patient's glycemic dynamics. Yet today, no clinical software tool tells the physician how old that sensor report has become, or whether its conclusions still hold true.

title: The Scientific Standard: The Reveal Protocol
section: SECTION A: OPENING & PROBLEM STATEMENT (Slides 1–8)
visual:
- Timeline Diagram showing the Reveal Protocol:

  - Temporal Firewall (Sensor Masked / Hidden from Twin)
  - Phase 2 (Days k+1 onwards): Estimation Window (Twin predicts glucose using only Meals + Record + Sparse Fingersticks)
  - Phase 3: The Reveal (True hidden sensor trace unmasked on top of Twin estimate)
- Pull Quote: "Calibrate on a few days of sensor data. Hide the rest. Estimate the hidden days without the sensor. Then lay the real trace on top."
narration: Faced with this clinical blind spot, we asked the central question that every medical digital twin claims to answer, but which almost none are willing to evaluate rigorously: if you calibrate a model on a few days of sensor data, and then take the sensor off, how accurately can you estimate the patient's glucose dynamics into the future? To answer this without deception, we instituted what we call the Reveal Protocol. We calibrate our digital twin on the initial days of a recording. We then erect a strict temporal firewall, hiding all future sensor data. Our twin must reconstruct the patient's glycemic trajectory using only their health record, meal logs, and occasional capillary fingersticks. Finally, we unmask the ground truth sensor readings and lay them directly on top. If the twin claims to know the patient's physiology, this is the only yardstick that matters.

title: The Clinical Landscape of Type 2 Diabetes Monitoring
section: SECTION A: OPENING & PROBLEM STATEMENT (Slides 1–8)
visual:
- Graphic: The Three Tiers of Diabetes Monitoring:
  - Tier 1: Quarterly HbA1c (Three-month weighted average, misses all glycemic variability and acute spikes)
  - Tier 2: Intermittent Self-Monitoring of Blood Glucose (SMBG/Fingersticks) (Point-in-time capillary measurements, painful, sparse)
  - Tier 3: Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) (Rich continuous curve, high cost, limited wear duration)
- Bottom Banner: "Chhaya bridges Tier 2 and Tier 3 by using sparse fingersticks to keep a prior CGM wear alive."
narration: To understand the medical necessity of our system, we must examine the limitations of current diagnostic tiers. HbA1c remains the clinical gold standard, yet it is merely a three-month weighted average. Two patients with an identical HbA1c of 7.5% can have completely different daily profiles: one maintains stable, gentle oscillations, while the other suffers dangerous excursions between severe nocturnal hypoglycemia and debilitating postprandial spikes. Self-monitoring via fingerstick meters captures snapshots, but misses peak excursions and nocturnal trends. CGMs provide the complete picture, but are fleeting. Chhaya bridges this critical clinical chasm. By leveraging sparse, low-cost fingersticks taken four to six times a day, Chhaya anchors and updates the physiological model established during that single fourteen-day sensor wear, giving the physician continuous insight without continuous sensor costs.

title: What Happens When a Sensor Report Ages
section: SECTION A: OPENING & PROBLEM STATEMENT (Slides 1–8)
visual:
- Diagram showing report staleness over time:
  - Day 0–14: Sensor Active (High confidence, valid AGP report)
  - Day 15–30: Moderate Staleness (Subtle therapeutic changes, dietary drift)
  - Day 30+: High Drift (Mean glucose shifts >20 mg/dL; old report leads to incorrect medication dosing)
- Callout: "In our held-out clinical data, mean glucose drifted by >20 mg/dL in 34% of patients following hospital care adjustment."
narration: What happens to a patient's glucose profile after the sensor comes off? In our analysis of clinical datasets, we uncovered a phenomenon that every endocrinologist suspects but rarely measures systematically: glycemic drift. In hospitalized and supervised patients whose medications were modified, glucose moved downward by approximately one milligram per deciliter per day. Within three weeks, a patient's mean glucose can diverge from their old ambulatory glucose report by more than twenty milligrams per deciliter. If a physician uses a thirty-day-old sensor report to titrate sulfonylureas or insulin, they are making dosing decisions on historical ghost data. The patient could be sliding into frequent nocturnal hypoglycemia, yet the static paper report on the doctor's desk still shows severe hyperglycemia. Chhaya was built specifically to detect and quantify this drift.

title: Defining a Medical Digital Twin
section: SECTION A: OPENING & PROBLEM STATEMENT (Slides 1–8)
visual:
- Contrast Graphic:
  - Left: "Marketing Twins" (3D animated human avatars, generic animations, black-box neural nets, uncalibrated confidence)
  - Right: "Chhaya Digital Twin" (Explicit physiological compartments, personalized metabolic parameters, Bayesian uncertainty bands, honest performance bounds)
- System Definition: "A parameter-personalized dynamical system mapping multi-scale inputs to physiological state estimates with calibrated uncertainty."
narration: In the tech industry today, the term 'digital twin' is too often degraded into marketing theater—a 3D rotating avatar of a human body hooked up to a black-box regression algorithm that outputs uncalibrated numbers. In medicine, an uncalibrated point estimate is worse than useless; it is actively dangerous. In Chhaya, we define a digital twin with scientific precision. Our twin is a parameter-personalized dynamical system of ordinary differential equations. It represents the biophysical transport of glucose from the stomach into plasma, endogenous pancreatic insulin secretion, peripheral glucose disposal, hepatic glucose production, and interstitial diffusion. It has seven identifiable personal parameters, and it never produces an estimate without an accompanying eighty-percent confidence band derived from a Laplace ensemble. It does not pretend to be omniscient; it shows exactly how certain or uncertain it is.

narration: Before we dive into the mathematics and code, we establish our intellectual contract—what Chhaya is, and explicitly what Chhaya is not. First, Chhaya does not claim to replace a physical continuous glucose monitor. When evaluated against capillary fingersticks on held-out patients, our estimate exhibits an error of approximately twenty-two percent, compared to twelve percent for a physical sensor. Second, Chhaya never recommends medication doses; insulin titration requires licensed clinical judgment. Third, Chhaya raises no alarms on estimated lows, because as we will prove shortly, open-source sensor data shows eighty-seven percent of sensor lows are false positives. Finally, we do not claim that fusing static medical records magically enhances sensor accuracy. By clearly stating these boundaries, we protect clinical safety and maintain absolute scientific integrity.

narration: Turning now to Section B, we examine the multimodal data architecture designed to fulfill Phase 1's core mandate: the seamless fusion of static historical records and dynamic real-time sensor streams. In clinical practice, these two sources exist in separate silos. The static record resides in hospital electronic health record systems—infrequent, structured, and retrospective. The dynamic stream resides on patient smartphones and wearable devices—high-frequency, noisy, and prospective. Chhaya unifies them through a mathematically principled Bayesian hierarchy. The static health record establishes the prior distribution over the patient's metabolic parameters. The dynamic wearable streams then act as the likelihood, updating the state space through continuous differential equations and discrete filter assimilation. Let us inspect each stream in detail.

The record captures core demographic variables—age, biological sex, body mass in kilograms, and calculated BMI. It details disease duration in years, current pharmacological therapy including oral hypoglycemic agents like metformin or sulfonylureas, and historical laboratory chemistry. Specifically, it ingests fasting plasma glucose and laboratory HbA1c measured from venous blood draws. In a clinical deployment, this module connects directly to hospital EHR systems via standard FHIR APIs, ensuring zero friction in patient onboarding.

title: Stream 2 (Dynamic/IoT): Continuous Glucose Monitoring Time-Series
section: SECTION B: DATA ARCHITECTURE — FUSION OF TWO STREAMS (Slides 9–18)
visual:
- Plot: Raw Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) Signal
  - Frequency: 5-minute sampling interval (288 readings/day)
  - Unit: mg/dL (converted internally to mmol/L for physics ODEs)
  - Physiological Delay Annotation: Interstitial-to-plasma transport lag (tau_g = 10.0 minutes)
  - Artifact Handling: Handling sensor dropout, non-physiological gradient clipping (>4 mg/dL/min)
- Formula Box: `dG_sub/dt = (G_plasma - G_sub) / tau_g`
narration: The first component of Stream 2 is the dynamic time-series generated by continuous interstitial glucose sensors. Modern sensors measure the enzymatic oxidation of glucose in subcutaneous interstitial fluid at five-minute intervals, producing two hundred and eighty-eight readings per day. However, interstitial glucose is not plasma glucose. There is a physiological transport delay of approximately ten minutes as glucose diffuses across the vascular capillary endothelium into the interstitial space. In our JAX model, as defined in `src/chhaya/twin/model.py`, this is represented by an explicit first-order lag compartment with time constant tau-g. Our ingestion pipeline filters sensor compression dropouts, handles missing data epochs, and validates signal continuity before passing the trace to our calibration engine.

title: Stream 2 (Dynamic/IoT): Capillary Blood Glucose (Fingersticks)
section: SECTION B: DATA ARCHITECTURE — FUSION OF TWO STREAMS (Slides 9–18)
visual:
- Illustration of Fingerstick Data:
  - Sparse sampling: 4 to 6 capillary measurements per day (Fasting, Pre-prandial, 2h Post-prandial, Bedtime)
  - Scale Difference: Capillary whole blood vs Interstitial enzymatic sensor
  - Calibration Function: Linear scaling function learned during the initial wear window:
    - `G_sensor_scale = alpha * G_meter + beta`
  - Table: Report Mean Glucose Error:
    - Raw Meter Average: 18.3 mg/dL error
    - Sensor-Scaled Fingerstick Average: 6.4 mg/dL error
narration: The second dynamic input stream consists of self-monitored capillary blood glucose—traditional fingersticks. While infrequent—typically taken four to six times a day around meals and bedtime—fingerstick measurements serve as high-integrity anchor points. But capillary meter glucose and interstitial sensor readings exist on different operational scales due to factory calibration differences. As documented in our decision record `2026-10-08-fingersticks-report`, taking a plain average of raw meter values misses the true sensor mean by eighteen point three milligrams per deciliter. However, by learning a simple linear transfer function during the initial shared wear period, Chhaya converts fingersticks to the sensor's scale, reducing the report error to just six point four milligrams per deciliter.

title: Stream 2 (Dynamic/IoT): Nutrition & Meal Ingestion Logging
section: SECTION B: DATA ARCHITECTURE — FUSION OF TWO STREAMS (Slides 9–18)
visual:
- Macronutrient Decomposition Diagram:
  - Input: Meal timestamp $t_{meal}$, Carbohydrate mass (grams), Fat/Protein/Fiber breakdown
  - Gut Appearance Model: Two-parameter Weibull absorption curve
  - Shape parameter $\sigma = 1.35$
  - Slowing factor: `meal_slow` computed from co-ingested fat and dietary fiber
  - Gut-to-plasma absorption rate: $k_1 / \text{meal\_slow}$
- Graph: Glycemic response of High-Carb/Low-Fat vs Identical Carb with High-Fat/Fiber (delayed, blunted peak)
narration: Dynamic metabolic simulation cannot occur without nutritional inputs. Stream 2 ingests event-based meal logs containing ingestion timestamps, total carbohydrate content in grams, and qualitative macronutrient composition. In real human biology, a hundred grams of carbohydrates from white rice creates a violent, rapid glycemic surge, whereas the same carbohydrate load eaten with dietary fat and fiber results in a blunted, protracted appearance curve. In `chhaya.twin.model`, we implement this physiology using a two-parameter Weibull distribution with shape parameter sigma equal to one point three five. A specialized parameter, `meal_slow`, acts as a divisor on gut emptying rate k1, dynamically modulating absorption speed based on co-ingested macronutrients.

title: Stream 2 (Dynamic/IoT): Physical Activity & Circadian Metrics
section: SECTION B: DATA ARCHITECTURE — FUSION OF TWO STREAMS (Slides 9–18)
visual:
- Multimodal Wearable Sensors:
  - Accelerometry & Heart Rate: Converted to continuous Metabolic Equivalent of Task (METs) per minute
  - Rest threshold: $\text{MET} < 1.5$ (basal metabolism)
  - Exercise time constant: $\tau_{ex} = 45.0$ minutes (prolonged insulin-independent uptake)
  - Sleep & Circadian Tracking: Circadian sinusoidal term on hepatic glucose output
  - Dawn Phenomenon Peak: 05:00 AM ($\text{minute} = 300.0$)
- Formula: $E_{ex}(t) = \int_0^t \max(\text{MET}(\tau) - 1.5, 0) \cdot e^{-(t-\tau)/\tau_{ex}} d\tau$
narration: Completing Stream 2 are wearable metrics of physical exertion and circadian rhythms. Continuous accelerometry, step counts, and optical heart-rate variability are converted into a continuous time-series of Metabolic Equivalent of Task, or METs. When energy expenditure exceeds one point five METs, Chhaya activates an exercise state variable that enhances insulin-independent peripheral glucose clearance with a forty-five-minute physiological recovery constant. Simultaneously, our model accounts for the well-known 'Dawn Phenomenon' observed in Type 2 diabetes. Using sleep detection from consumer wearables, the twin introduces a circadian cosine modulation on basal hepatic glucose output, peaking at five o'clock in the morning, successfully replicating morning fasting surges that baffle simpler models.

The second is state-level fusion: during the post-sensor phase, the physiological simulation runs forward driven by logged meals, while sparse fingerstick measurements assimilate into the running estimate via an exponential decay filter. Simultaneously, those same fingersticks are monitored against the sensor's baseline to detect clinical drift. This is true multimodal data fusion.

The first is ShanghaiT2DM, a high-fidelity inpatient study of one hundred Type 2 diabetic patients published in Nature Scientific Data. In this cohort, patients received supervised hospital care, daily medication titrations, five-minute CGM recording, and six reference fingerstick measurements per day. The second dataset is CGMacros from PhysioNet, capturing forty-five free-living individuals in the United States logging their unrestricted daily meals with continuous Dexcom sensors. Both datasets are downloaded directly via automated checksum-verified scripts without redistributing private patient traces, ensuring reproducibility and strict compliance with original data licenses.

narration: A fatal flaw in many published machine learning models is data leakage—either splitting by data row so the model memorizes future time points of the same individual, or tuning hyperparameters on the test set. In Chhaya, our engineering protocol makes leakage mathematically impossible. First, we split strictly by patient, never by row. Exactly half the patients in each cohort were assigned to development, and the other half were held out until the final evaluation. Second, every feature generation function in our test suite includes an automated zero-leakage test: it synthetically perturbs every single reading in the hidden sensor window and asserts that not a single bit of the estimated trace changes. Finally, our confirmatory runs require a dedicated `--confirm` CLI flag that aborts if uncommitted code is detected.

title: Algorithmic Core: The Augmented E-DES Physiological Engine
section: SECTION C: THE TWIN — ALGORITHMIC MODEL (Slides 19–32)
visual:
- Physiological Diagram: Four Biological Compartments:
  1. Gut Glucose ($Q_{gut}$): Meal ingestion, enzymatic breakdown, gastric emptying
  2. Plasma Glucose ($G_p$): Balance of gut absorption, basal hepatic production, renal clearance, and insulin-dependent uptake
  3. Plasma Insulin ($I_p$): Endogenous pancreatic beta-cell secretion (proportional + derivative response) and systemic clearance
  4. Interstitial Glucose ($G_{sub}$): Diffusion equilibrium between capillary bed and subcutaneous tissue (sensor interface)
- Reference: Maas et al. (2015), Erdos et al. (2023), implemented in `src/chhaya/twin/model.py`.
narration: We now enter Section C to examine the algorithmic heart of Chhaya: our augmented physiological engine. Rather than relying on opaque deep neural networks that output uninterpretable embeddings, Chhaya builds upon the E-DES differential equation model established by Maas and Erdos. The human glycemic control loop is modelled as a four-compartment biological system: oral carbohydrate ingestion into the gut, bi-directional glucose flux into circulating plasma, pancreatic insulin release driven by both absolute glucose concentration and its rate of change, and eventual diffusion into the interstitial fluid. To this established foundation, our team engineered two critical physiological expansions: a circadian hepatic driver to model dawn phenomenon spikes, and a muscular exertion uptake term driven by wearable MET activity.

title: Mathematical Compartments & Governing Differential Equations
section: SECTION C: THE TWIN — ALGORITHMIC MODEL (Slides 19–32)
visual:
- System of Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs):
  $$\frac{dQ_{gut}}{dt} = -k_1 \cdot Q_{gut}(t) + \text{Meal}(t)$$
  $$\frac{dG_p}{dt} = \frac{f \cdot k_2 \cdot Q_{gut}}{V_g} + G_{liv}(t) - (k_3 + k_4 I_p(t)) \cdot G_p(t) - R_{renal}(G_p) - U_{ex}(t)$$
  $$\frac{dI_p}{dt} = \beta \cdot [k_7 (G_p - G_b)^+ + k_8 \frac{dG_p}{dt}^+] - k_9 I_p(t)$$
  $$\frac{dG_{sub}}{dt} = \frac{G_p(t) - G_{sub}(t)}{\tau_g}$$
- Annotation: Captures renal threshold ($G_{th} = 10.0$ mmol/L) and derivative beta-cell secretion.
narration: Displayed here are the governing differential equations of our digital twin. Notice how physical conservation laws govern every state transition. Gut absorption is governed by rate constant k1. Plasma glucose concentration G-p is balanced by hepatic output G-liv, peripheral clearance driven by plasma insulin I-p, and renal glycosuria which activates whenever plasma glucose exceeds the ten millimole per liter renal threshold. Endogenous insulin secretion captures two hallmark biological behaviors: a proportional response driven by deviation from basal glucose G-b, and a derivative response driven by the velocity of glucose increase, mimicking early-phase secretory burst release from pancreatic beta-cell granules. This non-linear dynamical structure ensures that the virtual patient behaves within the bounds of human biology.

narration: A classic challenge in physiological modelling is overparameterization—if a model has forty unconstrained parameters, it can fit arbitrary noise but fails completely on out-of-sample data. In Chhaya, we solved this by fixing population-level constants such as glucose distribution volume and renal clearance based on published clinical literature, while isolating exactly seven personalized biological parameters denoted by vector theta. These seven parameters capture individual metabolic identity: how fast the stomach empties, how sensitive muscle tissue is to insulin, the patient's baseline hepatic setpoint, the magnitude of their morning dawn phenomenon, and their sensitivity to physical exercise. By transforming these variables through log and logit functions, we ensure mathematical stability and biological validity across all numerical evaluations.

title: Differentiable Simulation in JAX
section: SECTION C: THE TWIN — ALGORITHMIC MODEL (Slides 19–32)
visual:
- Architecture Box: JAX High-Performance Numerical Engine
  - Just-In-Time (JIT) Compilation: `jax.jit` compiling ODE integration down to GPU/XLA native machine code
  - Automatic Differentiation: `jax.grad` computing exact analytical gradients $\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}$ without finite-difference approximations
  - Vectorized Execution: `jax.vmap` enabling simultaneous multi-patient and multi-day evaluation
  - Precision: 64-bit floating point (`jax_enable_x64=True`) for numerical integration stability
- Speed Comparison:
  - Standard Python ODE (Scipy `solve_ivp`): ~1,400 ms per 14-day calibration
  - Chhaya JAX ODE (`scan`-based Euler-Heun): ~12 ms per calibration (>100x speedup)
narration: Executing complex physiological ODE simulations across thousands of patient days in a production application requires extreme computational efficiency. We implemented Chhaya entirely within JAX, Google's high-performance numerical framework. By structuring our ODE solver around `jax.lax.scan` and compiling via XLA, our simulation integrates a full fourteen-day time-series in just twelve milliseconds—over one hundred times faster than standard SciPy solvers. More importantly, JAX gives us exact automatic differentiation. We compute analytical gradients of our loss function with respect to all seven biological parameters simultaneously, enabling gradient-based optimization algorithms to converge in milliseconds without noisy finite-difference approximations.

title: Bayesian Calibration: MAP Estimation & Laplace Ensemble
section: SECTION C: THE TWIN — ALGORITHMIC MODEL (Slides 19–32)
visual:
- Diagram: Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) Optimization & Uncertainty Band:
  - Objective Function: $\min_\theta \left[ \frac{1}{2\sigma_e^2} \sum_{t} (G_{sub}(t; \theta) - G_{cgm}(t))^2 - \log P(\theta | \text{EHR}) \right]$
  - Prior $P(\theta | \text{EHR})$: Derived from static fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, and BMI
  - Hessian Matrix at Mode: $H = \nabla_\theta^2 \mathcal{L}(\theta^*)$
  - Laplace Approximation: $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta^*, H^{-1})$
  - 80% Prediction Band: Generated by drawing parameter samples from Laplace posterior and forward-simulating
- Visual: Purple shaded 80% confidence corridor surrounding the median estimate trace.
narration: Calibration proceeds via Bayesian Maximum A Posteriori estimation. During the wear period, the optimizer minimizes the sum of squared differences between simulated interstitial glucose and observed CGM readings, penalized by our Bayesian prior derived from the electronic health record. Once the optimal parameter vector theta-star is identified, we compute the Hessian matrix of second derivatives to evaluate the local curvature of the parameter space. Inverting this Hessian provides the Laplace approximation of parameter covariance. We draw an ensemble of parameter vectors from this posterior distribution and forward-simulate them, constructing an honest, calibrated eighty-percent confidence corridor. When the patient's data is noisy or sparse, the corridor naturally widens, alerting the clinician to elevated uncertainty.

title: Blending Physiology with Habit: The Dual Estimate Architecture
section: SECTION C: THE TWIN — ALGORITHMIC MODEL (Slides 19–32)
visual:
- Formula & Concept Diagram:
  $$\hat{G}_{\text{twin}}(t) = 0.50 \cdot G_{\text{physiological}}(t) + 0.50 \cdot G_{\text{average\_day}}(t)$$
  - Component 1: Physiological ODE Simulation ($G_{\text{physiological}}$)
    - Knows what the patient ate *today* (carbohydrate grams, meal timing, exercise)
    - Captures acute postprandial excursions
  - Component 2: Patient's Own Average Day ($G_{\text{average\_day}}$)
    - Non-parametric binned median daily profile learned from the 14-day wear
    - Knows habitual baseline habits, unlogged snacks, and unmeasured metabolic rhythms
- Graph: Showing how the blend smooths unlogged events while tracking real meal peaks.
narration: In real life, patients do not log every bite of food or every flight of stairs. If a digital twin relies solely on differential equations driven by meal logs, any unlogged snack will cause the model to miss the baseline entirely. Conversely, if a model relies purely on historical averages, it is blind to acute dietary variations. Chhaya resolves this tension through our dual-estimate architecture: our running estimate is a fifty-fifty blend of forward physiological simulation and the patient's own historical average day. The physiological branch provides acute responsiveness to logged meals and exercise. The average-day branch anchors the trace against unlogged habitual behaviors. On held-out testing, this blend significantly outperformed either single component alone.

title: Sparse Data Assimilation: The Fingerstick Filter
section: SECTION C: THE TWIN — ALGORITHMIC MODEL (Slides 19–32)
visual:
- Filter Architecture Diagram:
  - Input: Capillary fingerstick arrival at time $t_k$
  - Innovation / Error: $\Delta G = G_{\text{stick}}(t_k) - \hat{G}_{\text{twin}}(t_k)$
  - Exponential Nudge Filter:
    $$\hat{G}_{\text{assimilated}}(t) = \hat{G}_{\text{twin}}(t) + \Delta G \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{t - t_k}{\tau_{\text{decay}}}\right)$$
  - Decay Constant: $\tau_{\text{decay}} \approx 120$ minutes (2 hours)
  - Uncertainty Adjustment: Uncertainty band expands as time elapsed since last fingerstick grows
- Graph: Fingerstick diamond nudges the purple estimate curve, which gently relaxes back to baseline over 2 hours.
narration: Once the continuous sensor is removed, how does the twin stay grounded in current reality? Through sparse data assimilation. When the patient takes an occasional fingerstick, say before lunch or two hours postprandial, that single measurement provides ground truth at time t-k. As implemented in `chhaya.twin.assimilate`, we compute the innovation—the difference between the fingerstick and our prior estimate. The twin applies an exponential nudge that shifts the trajectory toward the true capillary value. This correction gently decays over a two-hour half-life, mirroring the physiological autocorrelation of human glucose kinetics. If the patient tests four to six times a day, the twin remains remarkably anchored to the patient's true metabolic trajectory.

We hypothesized that giving the twin the patient's static health record—specifically fasting lab glucose and HbA1c—to set parameter priors would significantly reduce error compared to population priors. On twenty held-out participants with only twenty-four hours of sensor data, incorporating the record altered estimation error by an imperceptible median of zero point zero two milligrams per deciliter, with a p-value of zero point one six. With three or more days of sensor wear, the benefit dropped to zero. What does this teach us? Once a patient wears a continuous physiological sensor for even seventy-two hours, the rich dynamic likelihood completely overwhelms the static medical record. The EHR provides crucial clinical context, but it does not refine physical ODE parameters.

title: Staleness Detection: CUSUM Drift Monitor

narration: One of our most impactful clinical features is the Staleness Monitor—an automated prompt alerting the physician when a patient's historical sensor report is no longer valid. Using a Cumulative Sum of fingerstick surprises against the baseline wear, the monitor separates clinically drifted recordings—defined as a shift in mean glucose exceeding twenty milligrams per deciliter—from stable recordings with an AUROC of zero point eight two. At our calibrated operating threshold, the system flags sixty-four percent of drifted patients within two point six days while maintaining a ten percent false-positive rate. Crucially, a simple comparison of fingerstick averages against the report also achieved zero point eight two. We report this tie openly: the plain baseline works just as well as the dynamic monitor.

title: Sensor Low Audit: The 12.5% Reality Check
section: SECTION C: THE TWIN — ALGORITHMIC MODEL (Slides 19–32)
visual:
- Results Card: **Sensor Label Validity Audit (`chhaya.data.audit`)**
  - Dataset: ShanghaiT2DM full paired dataset (sensor readings with simultaneous fingerstick within 10 minutes)
  - Evaluation of Hyperglycemia ($> 180$ mg/dL):
    - 809 sensor highs analyzed → **732 confirmed by fingerstick (90.5% true positive rate)**
  - Evaluation of Hypoglycemia ($< 70$ mg/dL):
    - 64 sensor lows analyzed → **ONLY 8 confirmed by fingerstick (12.5% true positive rate!)**
    - Nocturnal sensor lows ($< 70$ mg/dL at night): **0 of 9 confirmed (0.0% true positive rate!)**
- Design Consequence:
  - Sensor compression artifacts cause massive false lows.
  - Chhaya labels all sensor lows on UI as: **"Sensor low, unconfirmed"**. No low-glucose alarms are ever issued.
narration: Before moving to the user interface, we present a startling finding from our label audit that dictated our entire clinical safety design. Across hundreds of paired measurements where a fingerstick was taken within ten minutes of a sensor reading, sensor highs above one hundred and eighty milligrams per deciliter were confirmed ninety point five percent of the time. But for sensor lows below seventy milligrams per deciliter, only eight out of sixty-four were confirmed—an eighty-seven point five percent false positive rate. At night, zero out of nine sensor lows were confirmed. Why? Because when a sleeping patient rolls onto their sensor, physical tissue compression temporarily halts microvascular perfusion, creating artificial 'compression lows'. Had we trained a machine learning model to predict raw sensor lows, it would have learned to predict sleeping posture, not hypoglycemia. Therefore, Chhaya labels every sensor low on screen as 'unconfirmed', and refuses to generate automated low alarms.

title: The Limits of Physiology: The 2% Incremental Gain Reality

narration: Here is a humbling biological truth uncovered by our research: the incremental predictive benefit of complex physiological ODE modeling is small. When we decomposed our model's performance on held-out patients, ninety-four percent of the baseline predictive accuracy came from simply knowing the patient's habitual daily pattern—the average day. Adding logged meals improved accuracy by four percent. The sophisticated differential equations of the E-DES model added approximately two percent. While that two percent is statistically significant and clinically valuable for meal-specific what-if exploration, it demonstrates that in Type 2 diabetes management, human habit and consistent fingersticks do the heavy lifting. Mathematical models must be humble about their true contribution.

Under these conditions, glucose drifted downward by one milligram per deciliter per day. Indian outpatient care represents a distinct intermediate environment: patients consume higher-carbohydrate diets, exercise variably, and test their blood glucose only once or twice a day. We explicitly declare that Chhaya must undergo prospective validation in Indian outpatient clinics before deployment.

narration: Another crucial limitation lies in our uncertainty calibration. While our eighty-percent prediction band achieved an average coverage of eighty-three point five percent across the held-out cohort, individual coverage varied widely—from sixty percent in highly erratic patients up to ninety-eight point five percent in stable patients. Ten of nineteen patients fell within our targeted seventy to ninety percent corridor. When we attempted to apply an empirical scaling factor of zero point seven eight derived on our development cohort to sharpen the band, it failed to transfer to the test set, reducing coverage to seventy-five point seven percent. We immediately discarded the recalibration factor. Our band is calibrated on average across populations, not yet per individual.

title: What We Omitted and Why (Model Scope Boundaries)

visual:
- Explicit Architectural Boundary List:

  - ❌ **No Pharmacokinetics / Pharmacodynamics (PK/PD)**: Oral agents (metformin, sulfonylureas, SGLT2i) are captured via static priors, not active drug concentration equations.
  - ❌ **No Counter-Regulatory Hormonal Cascades**: Glucagon, cortisol, and epinephrine surges during stress/hypoglycemia are not explicitly modeled.

narration: To prevent any clinical misapplication, we explicitly document what our mathematical model omits. First, the ODE engine does not include exogenous insulin kinetics—it models endogenous pancreatic secretion, meaning it cannot simulate subcutaneous insulin glargine or lispro injections. Second, it does not incorporate explicit pharmacokinetics for oral medications; metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors are reflected in the patient's baseline sensitivity parameters, not dynamic blood drug concentrations. Third, we omit counter-regulatory hormonal cascades such as adrenaline and glucagon release. Finally, our cohorts do not capture the unique 'thin-fat' phenotype characteristic of South Asian Type 2 diabetes. Stating these scope boundaries clearly is essential for clinical safety.

title: The Value of Plain Baselines: When Simple Averages Rival Complex Models

narration: One of the most profound lessons of this project was the formidable power of plain, unsexy baselines. When reconstructing multi-day report mean glucose from fingersticks, our sophisticated differential equation filter achieved an error of eight point nine milligrams per deciliter. But a plain arithmetic average of those same fingersticks, converted to sensor scale, achieved an error of six point four milligrams per deciliter—beating our complex estimator! Similarly, in detecting drifted reports, our CUSUM filter tied exactly with a simple comparison of fingerstick averages at zero point eight two AUROC. In engineering, you must never assume complexity equals clinical superiority. We built the advanced models, tested them against simple baselines, and reported the results with total fidelity.
